summary:
Himāchal Pradesh has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own in the available sources; a visitor to the state operates under India's national framework, which the Parliament of India altered on 25 March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of reporting, with protests held in Mumbai on the day of passage.

The amendment removes the self-identification route established by the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling and narrows legal recognition to the male and female categories together with historically accepted socio-cultural identities such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex people. Trans men, trans women and non-binary or gender-fluid people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Recognition under the amended 2019 law requires certification from a medical board and a district authority before gender-affirming surgery, so access to legal recognition now runs through medical and administrative examination rather than self-declaration.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring people into being transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people.

India has an estimated two million transgender people, and critics of the amendment warn that the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people from recognition and from the welfare schemes tied to it.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity; there is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults under the new code.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.
tangentialFactors:
The Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Himāchal Pradesh is not among the states named in the sources as operating such a board.

The Allahabad High Court extended Article 15's prohibition in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds, a protection that rests on litigation rather than statute.

Intersex minors remain at risk nationally: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
localsOnly:
Residents of Himāchal Pradesh seeking legal gender recognition must satisfy the certification route introduced by the March 2026 amendment, which requires approval from a medical board and a district authority before gender-affirming surgery and confines recognition to male, female, traditional socio-cultural identities and intersex people.

Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Residents who self-identify outside the recognised categories fall outside the amended recognition scheme and, by extension, outside the welfare schemes conditioned on recognised status.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was still pending at the time of the sources; whether it has since been assented to and brought into force is unresolved here.

No Himāchal Pradesh-specific data on police conduct, healthcare facilities, welfare boards or documented incidents against trans people was found in the available sources, so the state-level picture is not sourced either way.

Whether the amended recognition scheme affects petitions or litigation already pending in Himāchal Pradesh is not sourced.

The characterisation of the new offences as echoing colonial-era criminalisation is an assessment by the People's Union for Civil Liberties, an advocacy organisation, and the assessment that police abuse is not systemic comes from a foreign government's country policy note; both are attributed positions rather than findings of a court.
